title: Occupational Health Risks and Health-Seeking Behaviours Among Healthcare Workers in Ghana: A Cross-Sectional Study of Three Facility Levels
content: Healthcare workers (HCWs) face multiple occupational hazards, but little is known about how they seek care and report injuries, particularly non-clinical staff and staff at lower levels of care in Ghana. This cross-sectional study surveyed 253 clinical and non-clinical HCWs at a health centre, a polyclinic and a district hospital in Ghana's Ashanti Region in May–June 2025. We examined factors associated with always seeking professional care after an occupational injury and with injury reporting using modified Poisson regression. Biological (65.6%), ergonomic (54.2%), and physical (51.8%) risks were most common and concentrated at the health centre (90.7%, 79.6%, and 88.9%, respectively). Almost half of respondents (49.0%) had been injured at work. Overall, 63.5% always sought professional care, with no difference by facility level or staff type; staff aged 31–40 years were less likely to do so than those aged 20–30 years (adjusted prevalence ratio 0.72; 95% confidence interval 0.57–0.92). Among injured workers, 70.2% had reported an injury; no independent predictor of reporting was identified. Occupational risks were common at all levels, and over one-third of HCWs sometimes self-medicated after injury. Implementing Ghana's existing health-sector occupational health and safety policy, especially at sub-district facilities, should be prioritised.
